passage:
At the clinic where they both worked as physiotherapists, Swati's engagement photos went round the staff room on Monday. Nazia was the loudest. "Gorgeous! You two are perfect!" She offered to cover Swati's Thursday shift, bought her a coffee and praised the ring three times before noon. By lunch her cheeks ached from smiling.
Rolling up a resistance band in the empty gym, she finally let herself think it: I'm jealous. Swati found someone, and I'm still being asked at every family dinner when I'll settle down. And I'm glad for her too. Both.
The breath she let out felt like her first real one all day. That afternoon, when Swati thanked her again, Nazia said simply, "I'm really happy for you. And a little envious, honestly."
Swati laughed and hugged her. "Envious is allowed."

qa.q: Which shift did Nazia offer to cover?
qa.a: Swati's Thursday shift.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling beneath the loud compliments?
qa.a: She was both envious and genuinely glad for Swati 😊; admitting the jealousy brought relief, like her first real breath all day.

qa.q: Why did admitting the mixed feeling help?
qa.a: Once Nazia named both envy and happiness, she no longer needed to overdo it, and one honest sentence made her kindness real.

qa.q: How does Swati respond to Nazia's honesty?
qa.a: Swati laughs and hugs her, saying envy is allowed, which suggests she feels closer to Nazia for being honest.

grounding: An adult who is overly sweet to a colleague she envies admits both envy and happiness, and her kindness becomes genuine.

subtype: Baby talk after a new sibling [Actor]
passage:
In the chilly week after Christmas, Kishore came back to kindergarten a different child. He had a new baby sister at home. At circle time he spoke only in baby words: "Me want milky." He wet his shorts, though he had been dry for a year. At pick-up he clung to Gargi Miss's dupatta and wailed, "Carry me!"
Gargi Miss knelt and held him close. "You're still my big Kishore, and I'll still look after you," she said. He sucked his thumb and leaned in.

qa.q: What did Kishore say at circle time?
qa.a: "Me want milky."

qa.q: Why might Kishore be talking like a baby again?
qa.a: He seems worried and unsure since his sister was born, and acting little is his way of checking there is still room for him to be cared for.

qa.q: How could his family and teacher support Kishore?
qa.a: Give him extra cuddles and one-to-one time without scolding the baby talk 🤍, and gently notice his big-boy skills, so he feels secure again.

qa.q: How might Gargi Miss see Kishore's change?
qa.a: She sees it as a need for reassurance, not naughtiness, which is why she kneels and holds him close.

grounding: A preschooler who was dry and speaking clearly returns to baby talk and clinging after his sister's birth.

subtype: Wanting to sleep near parents after a move [Actor]
passage:
The Delhi winter was a shock after Chennai. Two weeks after the move, Harish stood at his parents' door at midnight, holding his pillow. "Amma, can I sleep here? Just tonight."
Manjula lifted the quilt. It was the fifth "just tonight" that week. In Chennai he had packed his own school bag and fed the fish every morning. Now the bag lay half-empty by the door, and Manjula found herself feeding the fish.
At the new school, he told her, everyone spoke fast Hindi and laughed at jokes he didn't get. She didn't argue about the bag. At bedtime she oiled his hair the way she had in Chennai, and on Saturday they unpacked his posters together.

qa.q: What jobs did Harish do by himself in Chennai?
qa.a: He packed his own school bag and fed the fish every morning.

qa.q: Why does Harish keep asking to sleep in his parents' room?
qa.a: He feels lonely and unsettled at the new school, where he cannot follow the jokes, and being close to Amma soothes that stress.

qa.q: What small step would help Harish feel settled?
qa.a: Make his own room feel familiar, like unpacking posters together, and keep a calm bedtime routine so he slowly returns to his bed and jobs.

qa.q: What is it like for Manjula during these weeks?
qa.a: She takes on his jobs and her nights are broken, yet she chooses patience rather than arguing, trying to comfort him.

grounding: A child who has moved city and school asks to sleep in his parents' room and stops doing jobs he used to manage.

passage:
Before: On the hottest Saturday of the summer holidays, Chandrika came home from the state hockey selection trials, dropped her kit in the hall and went straight to bed. Her name wasn't on the list.
During: For two days she barely spoke. She wanted only curd rice with a spoon of sugar, the way Amma made it when she was small, and ate it under the blanket. When her brother Saurabh knocked, she said, "Go away." He left a mango outside her door anyway.
After: On Thursday evening Saurabh sat on the floor of her room and said nothing, just peeled a mango. Chandrika reached out for a slice. "I missed two easy passes," she said, and cried a little. Then she asked if he would practise with her after the rains.

qa.q: What did Chandrika want to eat?
qa.a: Curd rice with a spoon of sugar, the way Amma made it when she was small.

qa.q: Why did Chandrika stay in bed with childhood food?
qa.a: She felt crushed and ashamed after not being selected, and the old comfort food and blanket soothed her like when she was little.

qa.q: What helped Chandrika come back out?
qa.a: Saurabh's quiet warmth, leaving a mango and later sitting without pushing, gave her time until she was ready to talk and plan practice.

qa.q: How does Saurabh experience Chandrika's retreat?
qa.a: He is shut out at first but keeps quietly showing care, and finally gets to share her sadness and her plan.

grounding: A teenager who missed selection retreats to bed and childhood food, and warmth and time ease her back out.

subtype: Hostel student calling home in tears [Actor]
passage:
12 Dec, hostel, freezing.
Called Appa three times today. Three. Before the circuits exam, after the circuits exam, and at 10 p.m., because I couldn't find my warm socks and somehow that made me cry. He found them over video call ("left drawer, Lavanya, under the towels"). His name in my phone still says "Vijay Office" from years ago. Felt about nine years old.
Half my floor calls home too, I've noticed. Hema's mum sings to her on the phone.
Anyway. Something small: tomorrow's paper is maths, which I actually like, and I made my own revision chart without asking Appa what to do first. Didn't even think of calling about it.
Maybe the calls are like the socks. Something warm while it's cold. Maybe I'll need fewer after this week.

qa.q: Why did Lavanya call Appa at 10 p.m.?
qa.a: Lavanya could not find the warm socks, and that brought on tears.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling during that late call?
qa.a: Lavanya felt small and homesick, "about nine years old", needing Appa's comfort under exam stress.

qa.q: What small sign of growing confidence appears in the entry?
qa.a: Making a maths revision chart without asking Appa; noticing that step and building on it can make fewer calls feel natural.

qa.q: How might Appa feel about these calls?
qa.a: He likely feels glad to help and close to Lavanya, finding socks over video, though perhaps a little worried at how often the calls come.

grounding: A first-year student far from home calls a parent several times a day during exams while signs of confidence begin to grow.

passage:
Before: The week Lokesh started preschool, he began crawling to the table and asking for his milk in a bottle again. On Monday Thomas laughed. "You're too big for that!" Lokesh cried until dinner went cold.
During: By Wednesday Thomas tried something else. When Lokesh crawled in, Thomas scooped him up, gave him an extra-long cuddle and said, "Big day, huh?" The milk still came in his usual steel cup, and bath and story still happened at eight. Thomas didn't mention babies once.
After: The next Monday, Lokesh walked to the table, drank from the cup and told his father all about the class tortoise. At bedtime he asked for one extra cuddle, and Thomas gave him two.

qa.q: What did Lokesh ask to drink his milk from?
qa.a: A bottle.

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling when he changed his approach on Wednesday?
qa.a: After Monday's tears, Thomas seems regretful and tender, wanting to comfort Lokesh rather than tease him.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Extra cuddles without mocking, while keeping the steel cup and the eight o'clock routine, reassured Lokesh so he moved forward within a week 🙂.

qa.q: What was it like for Lokesh when Thomas laughed on Monday?
qa.a: He felt hurt and embarrassed, which is why he cried until dinner went cold.

grounding: A young father meets his son's baby-like behaviour with extra cuddles and no mocking while keeping routines steady.

passage:
Two days before Eid, the Hyderabad flat smelled of sheer khurma, but Ammi and Abbu were arguing in the kitchen about whose relatives would come first. Farida heard her own name somewhere in it, and her stomach clenched.
She grabbed her dholak and climbed to the terrace. She played the rhythm her teacher had taught, then faster, then harder, until her palms stung and her breathing slowed.
From the next terrace, Hrithik called, "That was loud!"
Farida grinned, a little sweaty. "That was angry," she said, and played one more round, this time soft and steady. When she went back down, the kitchen was quiet.

qa.q: What were Ammi and Abbu arguing about?
qa.a: Whose relatives would come first.

qa.q: Why did Farida play the dholak so hard and fast?
qa.a: She felt furious and anxious 😠 hearing her name in the argument, and pounding out the rhythm let the anger out in a safe, skilled way.

qa.q: What could help Farida after playing?
qa.a: Once calmer, she could tell Ammi or Abbu that the argument upset her, so she is not carrying it alone.

qa.q: How does Hrithik experience Farida's drumming?
qa.a: Hrithik simply hears it as loud, not knowing about the quarrel, and the friendly call lets Farida laugh.

grounding: A child furious about a family quarrel drums hard on the terrace until the storm passes.

passage:
That winter in Oslo, when the sun set before three, Kaito had already been warned twice by the hall warden for slamming doors and shouting at a flatmate over dishes. A friend dragged him to the university debate club, half as a joke.
Ulla, the club captain, handed him the side nobody wanted and gave him four minutes. Kaito went at it like a storm: fast, sharp, fists tight on the podium. When the bell rang, the room was silent, then applauding.
"Same fire," Ulla said afterwards, "but you only get four minutes, and you attack the argument, never the person."
By February, Kaito had a rule taped to his wall: argue hard, then shake hands. His flatmate noticed the doors had gone quiet.

qa.q: How long did Ulla give Kaito to speak?
qa.a: Four minutes.

qa.q: What might Kaito have felt when the room burst into applause?
qa.a: He probably felt surprised and proud, finding that the intensity which got him into trouble was welcomed within rules.

qa.q: What makes the debate club a good channel for Kaito?
qa.a: Clear rules, timed speeches and attacking arguments rather than people, honour his drive while keeping it safe; the taped rule carries that into daily life.

qa.q: How does Kaito's flatmate experience the change?
qa.a: The flatmate notices the doors have gone quiet, which suggests home feels calmer and less tense.

grounding: A young man with a fierce temper finds debating, where his intensity is welcomed within rules.

Pallavi: I don't really want to talk about home
Coach Nirmala: you don't have to tell me. is there someone you can talk to? the college counsellor is good
Coach Nirmala: tomorrow is a rest day. that's an instruction 🙂

qa.q: What time was Pallavi on the court?
What was Nirmala feeling about Pallavi's extra training?

qa.q: What balance does Nirmala suggest?
